name: Postural Restoration Institute (PRI)

card.summary: Therapist-taught breathing and asymmetry exercise system for posture; little published trial evidence.
card.note: Evidence base is mostly case reports and physiology papers.

quick.overview:
PRI is a posture method from physical therapist Ron Hruska built around breathing and body asymmetry.
The evidence base is thin, mostly case reports and basic physiology.
quick.mechanism: Specific breathing and positioning exercises aim to reduce asymmetric patterns and reposition the ribcage and pelvis.

lead: Postural Restoration is a posture-based approach to physical therapy developed by physical therapist Ron Hruska in the early 1990s. In 1999 he founded the Postural Restoration Institute (PRI) in Lincoln, Nebraska, to train other health professionals.[1] Practitioners use manual techniques and non-manual exercises, many centred on breathing and pelvic position, to reposition and retrain asymmetrical movement patterns toward what they call neutrality.[1]

For appearance, the draw is posture: people use PRI-style exercises hoping for more even shoulders, a less flared rib cage, a more neutral pelvis and a more upright, balanced stance, which changes how tall, lean and athletic someone looks. Advocates also say it improves breathing mechanics and movement, which can support better training.[1]
The published literature on the method consists mainly of case reports, descriptions of individual exercises and small trials in athletes and in people with low back pain.[2][3][4][5]

chain: Breathing and asymmetry exercises reposition rib cage and pelvis
Muscle patterns around the trunk and hips become more balanced
Stance looks more neutral and upright
angle.text: PRI exercises aim to correct one-sided postural habits such as pelvic shift, rib flare and uneven shoulders. People use them to stand more symmetrically and to train with better alignment, which shows in how upright and balanced they look.

Diaphragm function, zone of apposition, asymmetry patterns[1][3]

paras: Advocates say the body has built-in asymmetries, including a tendency to stand on the right leg and shift the centre of gravity to the right, and that these show up in the trunk, ribs, spine, pelvis and hips. PRI aims to restore neutrality and normal respiration through manual and non-manual exercises that reposition and retrain these patterns.[1][3]

Breathing is central. Practitioners refer to the diaphragm's zone of apposition, the region where the diaphragm attaches to the lower rib cage, and Wikipedia cites classic respiratory-mechanics papers by Goldman and Mead (1973) and Mead (1979) on how the diaphragm's action depends on its relationship with the rib cage.[1] A 2013 clinical paper describes what it calls a Left Anterior Interior Chain pattern, with a left rib flare, a decreased zone of apposition, and tight or weak muscle groups around the pelvis, and presents the right sidelying respiratory left adductor pull back exercise as a way to influence that alignment.[3]

Ron Hruska developed the method in the early 1990s, and in 1999 he founded the Postural Restoration Institute in Lincoln, Nebraska, to train healthcare professionals.[1] The institute teaches the method through courses to physical therapists, athletic trainers and strength coaches, and it is used in some sports-performance settings.[1] Wikipedia also lists a 2008 case study by Spence in a regional-anesthesia journal and a 2006 ethnography of the postural restoration subculture by Kyndall Boyle at Nova Southeastern University among its references.[1]

People interested in physique and posture use PRI exercises to address anterior pelvic tilt, rib flare and uneven shoulders, which can affect the silhouette of the waist, chest and back. Athletes also use the exercises for alignment before training. Practitioners describe the work as therapy delivered by trained clinicians, with home exercises prescribed afterwards.

A 2020 case report in the International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy described a 22-year-old collegiate volleyball player with unresolved right rotator cuff tendinopathy, bilateral rib cage flare and anterior pelvic tilt. Her previous shoulder programme was replaced with PRI exercises including a diaphragmatic breathing drill, a hamstring hip lift and the right sidelying respiratory left adductor pull back. Her pain rating fell from 6 to 2, the left hip gained 10 degrees of internal rotation, the right hip gained 14 degrees of external rotation and right shoulder internal rotation increased 15 degrees.[2]

A 2019 randomized controlled trial in 25 physically active male college students compared four weeks of non-manual Postural Restoration exercises with traditional posture exercises. The PRI group improved pro-agility times by 0.03 seconds (p=0.0005) and showed significant changes in femoroacetabular internal rotation and abduction symmetry and in the left adduction drop test; neither group improved vertical jump power.[4]

A 2021 randomized matched-subjects trial in 33 men with nonspecific chronic low back pain assigned participants to NASM (n=11), PRI (n=11) or combined (n=11) exercise programmes, three one-hour sessions per week for eight weeks, and found no significant differences between groups in pain, disability or movement control.[5] A 2013 article described the right sidelying respiratory adductor pull back exercise and its rationale.[3]

Wikipedia's article states that there is little strong evidence that any specific posture leads to better medical outcomes, citing a 2019 review by Korakakis and colleagues.[1] No published trial has measured visible posture, appearance or perceived height after a PRI programme.

timeline.event: Postural Restoration Institute founded in Lincoln, Nebraska.[1]
Clinical description of the right sidelying respiratory left adductor pull back exercise is published.[3]
Randomized trial of PRI exercises in 25 college men is published.[4]
Case report of PRI use in a volleyball player with rotator cuff tendinopathy is published.[2]
